I very nearly stayed up all night playing The Outlast Trials on my first outing with it, so that alone is worth a recommendation, but a lot of reviews so far aren’t really getting to what’s in this game, so I’ll take you on the tour of what I’m referring to as “Outlast-lite”.

The Outlast Trials (TOT) is a cooperative survival horror game. You and (optionally) up to three other players (friends, randoms or a mix) are thrown into spooky trials under the auspices of test subjects undergoing “therapy” at the hands of the Murkoff Corporation. You're given gruesome tasks to complete and you do these while avoiding or managing enemies that wander the maps. To aid you through this, you’ll find items sprinkled throughout the levels, and, additionally, you can select a loadout of perks and permanent upgrades that give you special abilities and boosts that you upgrade between missions, giving players the motivation to keep replaying maps.

And replay maps you will. TOT has three primary narrative maps that’re absolutely super. There's not much in the way of story, but you're taken on a good journey through each. The primary antagonist of each scenario is clearly presented, and the horror of what’s being asked of you is always deliciously entertaining. Furthermore, there’re six shorter missions that take place in different maps within similar tilesets to the primary ones. These don’t have as much story but do give the same gameplay taste and I thought they worked well as additional content that presumably took less development time. Finally, TOT offers a higher difficulty option for all the levels (though you unlock many of these later on), which adds difficulty modifiers (more damaging enemies, more traps, fewer items, etc.) that I think a lot of the levels really need once you get a bit of experience.

TOT is very much “Outlast-lite”. It has all the gruesome themes of the previous Outlast games, but what made the originals scary is precisely because you’re all alone in them. By contrast, TOT has an almost arcade-y feel to it, the gung-ho running around takes on a Left 4 Dead feel after a point, and there’s always another player near enough to bail you out of any messes you get yourself into. Even if you get downed you just go “oh well” and wait for someone to pick you up. Enemies never really scare you [i]per se[/i] because you get adequate warning that one’s seen you (even if you can’t exactly figure out where they are) and you can simply leg it for a room or two and then hide in a cupboard until they get bored and leave you alone. There’s the odd jump scare when a monster hiding in a locker throws itself out at you, or a gas pipe goes off next to you, but they’re very mild compared to the jump scares in the original games. Small caveat is that the tutorial is exclusively played solo and is arguably the scariest level in the game because of it, but if you can push through that then the rest is very tame.

However, TOT being Outlast-lite is possibly the exact twist that you, the nervous and anxious reader that prefers not to play horror games, needed to enjoy the series. You can simply cling together with your friends as you shuffle around the levels, constantly chattering for comfort as you go. That said, TOT is good at forcing players to split up, and the obtuse map design can make it difficult to meet back up again, particularly when you factor in the enemies roaming around. Overall, I maintain that TOT’s scare factor is generally much milder than its predecessors, If you think of it as a cooperative action game with a horror theme then you'll find it's not that dissimilar in feel to something like Left 4 Dead.

TOT’s most challenging element is navigating your way around. Each run at a level randomises some map elements including available pathways, breakable/trapped doors, objective locations and enemy spawns, so you’re always keeping watch for changes in each iteration. Map design itself is deliberately obtuse as several objectives require you to search the area to find objects you need to progress, and it’s stunningly easy to get lost. Experienced players will learn the maps in time, but starting out you’ll get lost a lot, and I think that’s all part of the fun. The voice chat works perfectly so you can ask others for help when you get stuck, or use the radial communication menu for a similar effect.

Map layout aside, you'll find the general difficulty of the game will drop off sharply after a few hours. There're some mission modifiers that make things more challenging, but most missions are very, very easy with a group of experienced players. Red Barrels critically need to look at ways to push the difficulty considerably because I've been in several groups that can clear the side missions in under five minutes and still get good individual player grades for it. It's actually more fun to have a mix of ability levels in your group because it slows the game down and allows you to immerse yourself in the theme and experience more. You only really get in trouble if you mistakenly end up in a dead end, or run into another enemy or series of traps while trying to escape an enemy. The harder difficulties punish mistakes more by making enemies do more damage, or by restricting your resources, but even those aren't meaningfully challenging if you've played enough to unlock them. The current matchmaking system groups you with players of a similar level of experience, so once you hit the level cap then levels will be trivialised by the combined experience of the group.

On the topic of matchmaking, it’s a bit of a mess. You’d think you’d pick a level and get matched with others looking for that level, but that’s not the case at all. It simply matches you with other players (admittedly very quickly) and then you either have to talk about what level you want to do, or just accept whatever level the group leader (decided randomly) picks. This system is fine if you don’t mind playing any random level, but it can get a bit frustrating if you’re trying to do something specific.

I’m not super qualified to talk about the solo experience (I’ve done 3 maps solo), but I can tell you that there’s a degree of scaling on the objectives (i.e. you do fewer), and you get infinite lives to retry a map with if you die. It works fine, but the game does feel like it was intended to be played multiplayer. You have adequate time to test solo play within the steam refund period if you want to try it out (should be enough time for the tutorial and one level at least).

Performance-wise, PC gamers have “enjoyed” a slew of unoptimised messes lately, but Red Barrels has pulled through with a beautifully optimised experience. It’s not bug free by any means, and some interactions get a bit quirky in moments, but my playthroughs have been really smooth. Very impressive stuff for releases at the moment. Furthermore, TOT is listed as Early Access, but there's a decent amount of gameplay here if you don't mind redoing the levels on the harder difficulties, and the whole package is so well put together I honestly feel they could've full released TOT as is and it'd have been acceptable.

Overall, I was very sceptical that a game concept like TOT would work, but developer Red Barrels have absolutely smashed it out the park. Arguably a better experience with friends, but I've played a majority of my games with randoms and I've had a lot of fun. What’s available at the moment is really impressive and I hope that they release more trials and challenges to build on this excellent foundation. If you’ve been nervous about playing a game in the Outlast universe then this is easily the most accessible because you can get others involved to help you.

Final note: the arm wrestling minigame in the lobby area is surprisingly entertaining.

Still, the game manages to surprise you from time to time — not with cheap jump scares, but with intense in-game situations and atmosphere.

The Outlast Trials goes beyond the norms of an immersive horror game, offering a blend of spine-chilling thrills and a deep sense of camaraderie. With its seamless gameplay, brilliantly designed challenges, and escalating tension, it stands out as a testament to the dedication of its creators. But what truly elevates this game is its ability to forge genuine connections amongst players.

A shining example of this was my encounter with a fellow gamer whose selfless actions created a memorable gaming experience. Despite remaining silent throughout, their commitment to our survival was loud and clear. Always stepping up to revive my buddy Justin and me, our teammate turned out to be a beacon of teamwork amidst chaos. When it was late in the night and we finally had to call it, their kind words promised more adventures, rounding off an exceptional session. The Outlast Trials is not just a game, it's a testament to the power of gaming to create meaningful bonds, even in the midst of horror. Highly recommended for the thrills and the friendships you'll forge along the way.

I love the horror genre; after playing the first Outlast (which is a gem, btw), I bought this game, and it was a great purchase.

It plays like Phasmophobia: you select a mission with your group, where you'll get some objectives to achieve while trying to survive the enemies on the map. However, I find it much better since the mechanics are more refined. Besides stamina and insanity, we also get noise and darkness meters.

Players also have personal talents, skills, and tools, making the game more cooperative. In your group, one player can take a tool to better fight enemies, another can bring a tool to heal the team, while a third can be more strategic and bring something to find objectives or open locks.

The game currently has many missions – I guess more than 30 – situated in various realms protected by unique bosses. Plus, the devs are constantly releasing new content, so it takes a while for the game to start feeling repetitive.

But guess what? They also have different modes in that case:

- Escalation mode: play missions till your team loses. The game starts easy and gets harder and harder.
- Make your trial: you can customize any mission.
- Invasion: impersonate the enemies and kill other players in this PvP mode.

Finally, microtransactions are almost nonexistent. All relevant content is free, just like all the battle passes, as long as you simply play the game. And tbh, the best skins are in the battle pass, not in the store, unlike other games.

The only drawback is the relatively small player base (I struggle to understand why).
But if you have friends to play with, I definitely recommend you try this game.

"Oh sh*it look at that!", — Outlast Trials is a co-op game with horror elements. The game is definitely better with friends, but you can also queue with randoms no problem.

Levels are filled with crazy enemies and deadly traps. The level design is next gen creativity, I have no idea how they came up with all these stories, but they are pretty insane. Your mission is to complete objectives and escape with your team. Unlike Dead by Daylight, where you can only repair generators, this game provides you with various objectives on each level. On some levels you have to steal the children, pour acid into the evidence, or electrocute the snitch. The game has a medium level of violence and it's pretty damn bloody, so please sensitive people be aware (!) <--

Gameplay wise, there are both long levels (an hour+ length) and short ones (about 15~ minutes). You have different perks and abilities, all of which can be upgraded using in-game currency. This currency can only be obtained by playing the game, which gives you a sense of progression and keeps you hooked. They also have character customization and cool skins.

It's a fun game for sure, and developers keep introducing new levels and events. Recently they have added a new feature to create your own levels, so overtime the game will get more and more updates, and community driven content!

One minute we’re laughing at someone else getting grabbed by an enemy, and the next I’m the one jumping out of my chair like my life genuinely depends on it. That being said, I’m pretty sure my doctor is starting to recognize me by now. I’ve never had so many near heart attacks from a single game. Outlast Trials is a cooperative horror game that initially offers a fun and new experience. However, this novelty wears off after a few hours. The challenges become repetitive, often using "reskinned" elements, and the current content feels a bit short. It's worth noting, though, that the developers are improving this with each season, adding new maps, challenges, and even new threats.

The game is good for a casual weekly play session. But dedicated players who complete all trials might find it repetitive and lacking new content after about 25 hours. The game would greatly benefit from more trials, new and varied challenges (not just "reskins"), and more enemy types. It's likely this problem will lessen over time, but we don't know when. This is a problem for players who get hooked and want each game to feel different from the last.


Outlast Trials has a prestige system similar to Call of Duty. You play, reach level 100, and then "prestige" to get certain rewards. There are also "rebirths," which are special trials you can do for more rewards.


One great thing about this game is its microtransactions. Currently, the game only has DLC, and there's no in-game currency you can buy with real money. The DLCs are mostly just skins, which are good for their price.

The game doesn't have a battle pass. Instead, it uses "catalogs." Each season adds a permanent catalog that you can get even if you play four seasons later. However, there are also limited-time catalogs. This is great because it offers some "exclusive" items without creating "FOMO" (Fear of Missing Out).


The game also includes a trial creation tool. Unfortunately, this tool is disappointing. It was presented as a true map creator, like Fortnite's Creative mode, but it only lets you use existing maps with custom modifiers. This limitation is a big letdown. A big change is needed to make it as versatile as Fortnite's editor. This would bring much-needed life and freshness to the game, letting players create varied maps with one or more objectives.


Regarding Season 4, which this review is based on, I think it's a good update. It brings a new map and a new enemy that presents an interesting threat. As always, it adds a catalog that I like. They also brought back the rebirth system and improved it. Now you can do rebirths with friends, and I hear it's more random, so there's always something new to look forward to.


I give the game an 8/10. The price is fair, and it's best to buy it when it's on sale for the most value. There's hope that Red Barrels will keep supporting the game with future content updates.

The Outlast Trials is a great addition to the Outlast series; even with multiplayer it stays true to its roots. It's  easy to pick up and lose hours to.

This keeps the co-op gameplay immersive and justified which is always something you worry about when Multiplayer is added to a Single Player game. It manages to maintain the dark, body horror unsettling atmosphere that defines the series.

At its core, the gameplay loop is simple: you enter a trial, complete various tasks, then are granted the ability to escape - all while more and more enemies spawn. Within the maps; there are tasks like the radio frequency finder which is more then just get item A for location B - however most of the time it feels like the minigame is find X Randomized Key in X randomized location.

The level design is excellent, rewarding players who learn the maps and master their layouts. Randomized elements—like door placements and item locations—keep each playthrough fresh, and one thing I enjoy is that the difficulty curve changes based on player count so you can enjoy the game alone if you want the original Outlast feel.

With that being said; replayability is a strong point. Varied loadouts, rigs, perks, and skills allows the maps you play over and over again to be tackled differently, as well various challenges and developer-led events introduce twists. 

The game has "battle passes" but unlike some ingame monetization aspects; I found this one respects the player’s time, with fair rewards for playing the game, good cosmetic unlocks and incentives to keep playing even after freeing your character. I don't feel "scammed", finishing trials gives plenty of rewards. 

If there’s a downside, it’s that with enough experience, the fear factor starts to diminish. You begin to see through the horror to the mechanics underneath, turning it into more of a calculated process rather than a pure survival nightmare.

[h1]The Outlast Trials[/h1]

[h3]First Impressions[/h3]
When I first heard that Red Barrels, the creators of the first two [i]Outlast[/i] games, were planning to make a co-op game in this universe, I was skeptical. I thought it wouldn’t capture the dreadful atmosphere of the originals. However, when I got access to the closed beta on October 28, 2022, I completely changed my mind. This game truly surprised me in a great way! What I found wasn’t just something different, it was a fresh, terrifying evolution of [i]Outlast[/i].

[h3]What’s the Story?[/h3]
The game is set in a dark Cold War-era facility where the evil Murkoff corporation conducts brutal psychological experiments on humans. The player takes on the role of one of the test objects, trying to survive the terrifying trials and uncover the corporation's dark secrets, through documents available in the game.

[h3]Gameplay[/h3]
• The game's core mechanics focus on stealth and survival, with limited items to scavenge along the way and no real combat, aside from throwing bottles or bricks at enemies to stun them.

• Trails can be experienced solo or in cooperative mode, where you can team up with up to four players for a more intense and dynamic experience.

• Character progression is key, with a max level of 99. As you play, you can unlock permanent upgrades, like faster stamina regen, health recovery, or more inventory space etc. There are 6 rigs (classes) to choose from: Stun, Blind, Heal, X-Ray, Barricade, and Jammer. You can also unlock perks in three categories: tool, skill, and medicine. All of this is designed to make gameplay easier and more enjoyable.

[h3]Graphics and Audio[/h3]
Red Barrels did a great job with the visuals, creating a unique and terrifying atmosphere that adds to the tension of the game. The sound fits well with the [i]Outlast[/i] series, it's not bad, and it helps create a creepy, immersive environment. For me, it's not too scary, but it definitely sets the right vibe.

[h3]Final Thoughts[/h3]
Overall, [i]The Outlast Trials[/i] sets a new standard for horror games with a co-op twist. Whether you're playing alone or with friends, it offers hours of exciting and intense gameplay. If you're looking for a fun and thrilling experience, this game won’t let you down. It's also well-optimized for Steam Deck, offering smooth performance on the go.

Final Score: 9/10

Psychopaths exhibit these personality traits that make them seem silly and funny but don't detract from how menacing and bloodlust they are. The levels are limited; with only two bosses and a few maps, there is little content yet. The game relies on repetition to get good scores and unlockables to keep you engaged. It is in Early Access, and you can tell, as there are bugs such as the game not registering inputs or foes getting stuck and not moving. However, these were rare. There is a need for more content to make the title feel more diverse and keep the tension going, as once you learn the maps, it's more of a game of how fast you can clear them.

The layout could have also been more intuitive, as some input combinations can be forgotten mid-chase.

[h1] Art Design and Visuals [/h1]
Visually it looks great; it is Outlast, after all. The presentation is there, and the maps are interesting; on the first try is a fight for survival, while subsequent ones are challenging to get that good evaluation score. The fear aspect is there, but it evaporates the more you play, which is a shame for a title with such attention to detail.

The graphics are good-looking, and the models are well done; some aspects are mixed from the story into the visuals. Evaluations give a performance to the player that tells them everything they did right and wrong as constructive feedback, allowing them to improve at the game. Most such improvements depend on the visual factor, seeing things on the screen and learning from the environment. Search for items, see which hallways are safer, or plan an escape route. Seeing a window and thinking, "Won't that make enough noise to attract foes?" changes the approach to gameplay through visual cues, which is fantastic!

[h1]Sound, Replayability and Performance[/h1]
The voice acting is funny, particularly Mrs. Gooseberry. It is so enjoyable listening to her chit-chat with the puppet she carries. The quality is fantastic, and it has moments, as Mr. Daddy can tell you to run when Gooseberry is near or the locals beating you up while complaining about the most random things. It finds a way to get a chuckle out of you every time.

The game's sound effects are diverse; it counts a massive selection of sounds and visuals to increase the player's immersion. Screams are piercing and loud while being under the effect of psychosis changes how the world is perceived as sounds, and the screen becomes distorted. These touches add more richness to the Outlast Trials experience. 

On replayability, the game is enormous. Each map has multiple challenges to accomplish, but even more important, it has an EXAM version of the trial. These add insane modifiers to make your odds of surviving low, and it changes the dynamic of gameplay so much it feels like a new game at times. From doors that open and close mechanically to fewer spots to hide in or other surprises, I let you discover them as they add a lot to a game with few maps, which is appreciated.

At first, I was pretty skeptical about the idea of a multiplayer set in the Outlast universe, but I have to admit, the developers did an excellent job of translating the series’ single-player mechanics into a multiplayer game. Where the older Outlast titles mostly relied on linear maps, The Outlast Trials offers sandbox-style environments that are cleverly interconnected. This bodes well for the potential scale and variety we might see in Outlast 3. Right now, The Outlast Trials features nine maps, all detailed and genuinely engaging. Each one contains a “Trial,” the main mission you need to complete at least once to get a grasp of the game’s narrative (though, to be honest, there isn’t much to decipher story-wise). Beyond the main Trials, there are also challenge missions set in the same maps but with different objectives, which add variety and extend the game’s longevity.

You can play the whole game solo, essentially like a traditional single-player Outlast game. And from what I’ve seen, there aren’t really any penalties or major balancing issues when playing alone. In fact, the tension is even higher when you know you can’t rely on anyone else and are surrounded by grotesque monstrosities (with some fantastic creature design). That said, the game really shines when played with friends or other players online. Sure, the tension drops a little (you can usually be revived by teammates and even brought back with rare syringes), but the teamwork makes it a lot more fun and some missions are clearly designed with co-op in mind (like when you need to find and carry multiple boxes).

If you’re looking to replay the game multiple times, I’d definitely recommend doing it with others. Just make sure to bump the difficulty up to “Intensive,” because the standard difficulty becomes far too easy with four players once you’ve learned the basics. Naturally, higher difficulties come with better rewards, mostly skins and in-game currency you can spend to unlock new active/passive abilities and cosmetic items both for your character and for your personal bedroom (yes, you get your own customizable space).

One of the best things is that items you’d expect to be locked behind a battle pass in other online multiplayer games can actually be earned just by playing and spending in-game currency. It’s a refreshing, player-friendly choice that really deserves praise. On the downside, something that doesn’t deserve much praise is the use of AI in content creation. It’s not entirely clear how extensively AI has been used, but it’s obvious in certain posters or photos (you’ll spot odd windows or strangely shaped fingers/legs if you look closely at the details). I just hope this doesn’t extend to more important content like skins and enemies.

So far though, the game has surprised me, maybe because I went in with low expectations. But honestly, with the strong mechanics it offers, it deserves a larger player base. Of course, it’s also on the developers to keep the community engaged with new content (and ideally with less AI involvement). If you enjoyed Outlast, I’d recommend giving this one a shot when you find it on sale.
